title: The hierarchical lattice
subtitle: An ultrametric group whose blocks fall into L^d congruent children.
summary: The hierarchical lattice is the direct sum of countably many copies of (Z/LZ)^d, with an ultrametric whose balls have exactly L^(dn) points. Each ball splits into L^d congruent children, every pair of vertices in different children of a ball sits at the top distance of that ball, and power kernels are summable exactly when their exponent exceeds the dimension. These three facts are what make block decimation close on one-variable laws.
text:
The hierarchical lattice $\mathbb H^d_L$ is the abelian group of finite sequences with entries in $(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, carrying the ultrametric in which two vertices are at distance $L^k$ when the last coordinate at which they differ is the $k$-th. Its balls are nested subgroups, of exactly $L^{dn}$ vertices at radius $L^n$, and each ball splits into $L^d$ congruent children. Every pair of vertices in different children of a ball lies at the top distance of that ball, so a coupling that charges each pair according to its distance charges all pairs between two children at one rate, which depends only on the two block sums. This is the structure that makes block decimation an exact operation on a single variable, and it is why the model appears throughout the rigorous theory of the renormalisation group [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. The lattice was introduced by Dyson (1969) as a one-dimensional model with long-range couplings in which a phase transition can be proved [@dyson-1969], and the group-theoretic description used here, with balls as cosets of nested subgroups, is the form in which the renormalisation group is usually set up [@bleher-sinai-1973]. A power kernel $\lVert xVert^{-d-\alpha}$ is summable exactly when $\alpha>0$, so the model with such a kernel is a long-range spin system with a finite interaction range in the only sense that matters: the total intensity at each vertex is finite. Two conventions are worth fixing at the outset. The dimension enters the lattice only through the block volume $m=L^d$ and the decay ratio $\lambda=L^{d+\alpha}=mL^{\alpha}$; any integer $m\geq2$ and any ratio $\lambda>m$ arise from some pair $(d,\alpha)$ once a scale $L$ is chosen. And the lattice is a group, so distances are translation invariant and every vertex looks like the origin. title: Hierarchical spin systems and decimation
subtitle: The block spin of a hierarchical model is distributed as a functional of independent copies of the block spin one scale down.
summary: A spin system on the hierarchical lattice with couplings constant on levels has a Hamiltonian that splits into the Hamiltonians of its children plus one interaction between their sums. Consequently the partition function and the law of a block spin are recovered from the law one scale down by an explicit operation, the free energy has an exact recursion, and the whole renormalisation group is a recursion on one-variable laws.
text: A hierarchical spin system is a spin model on $\mathbb H^d_L$ whose coupling between two vertices is a function of their level alone, so that the coupling at level $k$ has one value $J_k=JL^{-(d+\alpha)k}$. Its energy on a block splits exactly into the energies of the children of that block plus a single interaction between the child sums: pairs inside a child are at levels below the top, pairs in different children are all at the top level, and no pair inside the block is at a level above it. The partition function therefore factorises, and the law of a block spin is the image of the law one scale down under an explicit operation — block decimation — which acts on the single variable $\sum_{x\in\text{child}}\sigma_x$. This article states that identity, its iterates, and the free energy recursion that follows; the operation itself is studied in the next article and solved exactly in the Gaussian case . The identity is what is special about the lattice: on $\mathbb Z^d$ a decimation step produces an interaction that depends on the shape of the boundary between blocks, whereas here it produces one number per block. The structure is Dyson's (1969), who introduced the hierarchical approximation to prove a phase transition for power-law couplings [@dyson-1969], and it is the setting of the renormalisation analysis of Bleher and Sinai [@bleher-sinai-1973]. Only free boundary conditions are used, so every object below is finite-dimensional and every identity is exact at finite volume. Definitions and setting # Fix integers $L\geq2$, $d\geq1$ and a real $\alpha>0$, write $m=L^d$, and let $J>0$. Let $\varrho$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with $\int\sigma^2\varrho(d\sigma)<\infty$; the two cases used below are the Ising prior $\varrho=\tfrac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)$ and the Gaussian prior $\varrho=N(0,1)$. Spins are real numbers $\sigma_x$. For finite $S\subset\mathbb H^d_L$ and $\beta\geq0$, the hierarchical Hamiltonian is $$H_S(\sigma)=-\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset S}J(\lVert x-y\rVert)\sigma_x\sigma_y,\qquad J(L^k)=J_k=JL^{-(d+\alpha)k},$$ the partition function and Gibbs measure are $$Z_S(\beta)=\int_{\mathbb R^S}\exp\bigl(-\beta H_S(\sigma)\bigr)\prod_{x\in S}\varrho(d\sigma_x),\qquad \mathbb P_S(d\sigma)=\frac{e^{-\beta H_S(\sigma)}}{Z_S(\beta)}\prod_{x\in S}\varrho(d\sigma_x),$$ and the block spin of $S$ is $S_S=\sum_{x\in S}\sigma_x$. For $n\geq0$ put $Z_n=Z_{\Lambda_n}$, $\mathbb P_n=\mathbb P_{\Lambda_n}$ and $\mu_n$ for the law of $S_{\Lambda_n}$ under $\mathbb P_n$, so that $\mu_0=\varrho$. Pairs at level $k$ are those in different children of a common level-$k$ block, by the child decomposition , so the Hamiltonian may be regrouped by level. That regrouping is the first statement. Proof of the level decomposition Every pair $\{x,y\}\subset\Lambda_n$ lies in a unique pair of children, since the children partition $\Lambda_n$. If $x,y$ lie in the same child, the child is a coset $e_n(a)+\Lambda_{n-1}$ and levels are translation invariant, so the pair's level is at most $n-1$; the term it contributes is one of the pairs summed by $H_{\Lambda^{(a)}}$, and conversely every pair of a child is a pair of $\Lambda_n$ with the same level. title: The renormalisation group map
subtitle: Decimation as an operator on one-variable laws, and the scaling that makes it autonomous.
summary: Block decimation sends the law of a child's block spin to the law of the parent's: a nonlinear operator on probability measures on the line, a Gibbs tilt of a product measure followed by summation. Rescaling the spin by L to the power minus (d+alpha)/2 makes the operators at different scales into powers of a single map, whose fixed points and linearisations carry the critical behaviour.
text: Block decimation turns the exact recursion of a hierarchical spin system into an operator $\mathcal T_b$ on probability measures on the line: take $m$ independent copies of a law, tilt them by $\exp(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'})$, and record the law of their sum. The model applies $\mathcal T_{\beta J_n}$ with $J_n$ decaying geometrically, so the sequence of operators is not autonomous; rescaling the spin by $L^{-\theta}$ with $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$ multiplies the coupling by $L^{2\theta}$ at each step and makes the composition a power of one map $\mathcal R_\theta$. That map is the object whose fixed points, and whose linearisation at them, carry the critical behaviour: a fixed point is a self-similar block-spin law, and the eigenvalues of the derivative there are the exponents, in the way made precise in the article on exponents . Two of its properties are used constantly and are proved here: it commutes with dilations, in the sense that $\mathcal T_b$ applied to a dilated law is the dilation of $\mathcal T_{b\lambda^2}$ applied to the law, and it is continuous on laws supported in a fixed compact set. The construction is that of Bleher and Sinai (1973), who studied the transformation directly for Dyson's model [@bleher-sinai-1973], and it is the map developed from scratch in the renormalisation-group treatment of lattice field theory [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. Nothing in this article depends on the model being Gaussian or Ising; the two cases are worked out in the Gaussian article and, in its own form, in the percolation article . Definitions and setting # Write $A$ for the index set of children, of cardinality $m=L^d$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $b\geq0$ put $$Z_b(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^m}\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a with the convention that the integral is $+\infty$ when it diverges. The decimation operator is defined when $0<Z_b(\mu)<\infty$ by $$\mathcal T_b\mu(A')=\frac{1}{Z_b(\mu)}\int_{\mathbb R^m}\mathbf 1_{A'}\Bigl(\sum_{a\in A}s_a\Bigr)\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a for Borel $A'\subseteq\mathbb R$, and the scaled decimation operator at exponent $\theta>0$ is $$\mathcal R_{\theta,b}\mu=\bigl(s\mapsto L^{-\theta}s\bigr)_*\bigl(\mathcal T_b\mu\bigr),$$ the image of $\mathcal T_b\mu$ under multiplication by $L^{-\theta}$. The quadratic form of the tilt is $\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}=\tfrac12\bigl(\bigl(\sum_as_a\bigr)^2-\sum_as_a^2\bigr)$, so the tilt rewards configurations whose sum is large in absolute value. If $\mu$ is supported in $[-K,K]$ then $0<Z_b(\mu)<\infty$ for every $b\geq0$, because the exponent is bounded on $[-K,K]^m$; and $\mathcal T_b\mu$ is then supported in $[-mK,mK]$. For a law with tails heavier than Gaussian the normaliser can diverge, and then the operator is undefined at that $b$; the Gaussian case in the next article locates the threshold exactly. Dilation covariance and continuity # Two properties make the operator usable: it scales in a fixed way when the input is dilated, and it is continuous in the input law. For $\lambda>0$, with $\lambda_*\mu$ the law of $\lambda s$ under $\mu$, $$\mathcal T_b(\lambda_*\mu)=\lambda_*\bigl(\mathcal T_{b\lambda^2}\mu\bigr),\qquad \mathcal R_{\theta,b}(\lambda_*\mu)=\lambda_*\bigl(\mathcal R_{\theta,b\lambda^2}\mu\bigr).$$ Proof of dilation covariance Sampling $s_a$ from $\lambda_*\mu$ is the same as writing $s_a=\lambda t_a$ with $t_a$ sampled independently from $\mu$. The exponent becomes $b\lambda^2\sum_{a<a'}t_at_{a'}$, the normaliser becomes $Z_{b\lambda^2}(\mu)$, and the sum becomes $\lambda\sum_at_a$. Hence the law of $\sum_as_a$ is the image under multiplication by $\lambda$ of the law of $\sum_at_a$ computed with coupling $b\lambda^2$, which is the first identity. Multiplying by $L^{-\theta}$ afterwards gives the second, since dilations commute. title: The Gaussian renormalisation group
subtitle: On Gaussian laws the decimation closes on the variance, and the critical fixed point has multiplier L to the alpha.
summary: For a Gaussian prior, the law of a block spin stays Gaussian and its variance obeys a fractional linear recursion that is solved in closed form. The critical intensity is the reciprocal of the total kernel mass, the susceptibility is exactly beta_c over beta_c minus beta, and the recursion, written in the dimensionless coupling, has a nonzero fixed point with multiplier L to the alpha; hence the correlation-length exponent is one over alpha and the two-point exponent is two minus alpha.
text: With a Gaussian single-spin prior the decimation operator preserves Gaussianity: the tilt is quadratic and the sum is linear, so the block spin of a Gaussian model is Gaussian and the whole orbit is described by one number, its variance. The recursion for that variance is fractional linear, so it is solved in closed form: the block-spin variance at scale $n$ is $L^{dn}$ divided by $1-\beta\sum_{x\ne0}J(\lVert x\rVert)$ truncated to the first $n$ shells. Three consequences follow without further work. The critical intensity is the reciprocal of the total kernel mass, so the interaction is summable exactly in the regime in which the intensity is finite; the susceptibility is exactly $(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}\beta_c$; and the recursion written in the dimensionless variable $u_n=\beta J_nv_n$ has a nonzero fixed point whose multiplier is $L^\alpha$. The multiplier is the point of the exercise. In the dictionary of the exponent article , a multiplier $\lambda_1=L^\alpha$ at the critical fixed point gives $\nu=\log L/\log\lambda_1=1/\alpha$, which is the classical long-range value; together with the block-spin growth exponent $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$, which the normalisation of the recursion at the autonomous scale forces, it gives $\kappa=\alpha$ and hence $\eta=2-\alpha$. These are the values tabulated for long-range interactions by Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972], and they are exact for this model. The Gaussian model is the one case of the hierarchical recursion that is solved in closed form, and it is the reference point for the others: the non-Gaussian fixed point of Bleher and Sinai merges with it at $\alpha=d/2$ and governs the critical behaviour above that value, and the percolation exponents of the percolation article coincide with the Gaussian ones in the sense that its two-point exponent is also $2-\alpha$. The measure $\mathbb P_n$ is then a centred Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^{\Lambda_n}$ and $\mu_n=N(0,v_n)$ with $v_n=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_n}[S_{\Lambda_n}^2]$. Write $A$ for the operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb H^d_L)$ of convolution by the kernel $x\mapsto J(\lVert x\rVert)$, and $A_n$ for its compression to $\Lambda_n$, that is the symmetric matrix $A_n(x,y)=J(\lVert x-y\rVert)$ for distinct $x,y\in\Lambda_n$ and zero on the diagonal. Two quantities organise the computation. The coupling at level $n$ is $b_n=\beta J_n=\beta JL^{-(d+\alpha)n}$, and the dimensionless coupling is $u_n=b_nv_n$. The ratio of successive couplings is $\lambda=L^{d+\alpha}$. Closure and the variance recursion # Let $b\geq0$ and let $\mu=N(0,v)$ with $v>0$. If $bv(m-1)<1$ then $Z_b(\mu)<\infty$ and $$\mathcal T_b\mu=N(0,v'),\qquad v'=\frac{mv}{1-bv(m-1)};$$ if $bv(m-1)\geq1$ then $Z_b(\mu)=\infty$ and $\mathcal T_b\mu$ is undefined. title: Critical exponents from the renormalisation group
subtitle: Two numbers from the fixed point, and the algebra that turns them into the exponents.
summary: The exponents of a hierarchical model are read off from its fixed point: one from the multiplier of the linearised map, giving the correlation-length exponent, and one from the growth of the block spin, giving the susceptibility exponent and hence the two-point exponent. The scaling relations are then algebra, and hyperscaling is the one hypothesis that is not automatic.
text:
A model with a renormalisation-group fixed point has two numbers that matter: the multiplier $\lambda_1$ of the linearised map at the fixed point, which says how fast a perturbation of the critical intensity is amplified per scale, and the growth exponent $	heta$ of the block spin at criticality, which says how large a block's magnetisation is at scale $L^n$. The first gives the correlation-length exponent through $
u=\log L/\log\lambda_1$; the second gives the susceptibility exponent $\kappa=2	heta-d$, which is the same as the statement $\eta=2-\kappa$. Every other exponent follows from these two by algebra, provided the standard scaling hypotheses hold; hyperscaling is the one that can fail, and it fails in the classical regime of percolation. The hierarchical model contributes something that the Euclidean theory does not have: the growth exponent is not free. Because the recursion is autonomous only at $	heta=	frac12(d+\alpha)$, as the map article shows, any fixed point of the rescaled recursion with a finite nonzero variance has $	heta=	frac12(d+\alpha)$, so $\kappa=\alpha$ and $\eta=2-\alpha$ for every fixed point of this model. The nontrivial exponent is $
u$; in the Gaussian case it takes the classical value $1/\alpha$, and at the Bleher–Sinai fixed point it does not. For percolation on the hierarchical lattice both statements are theorems: the two-point exponent is $2-\alpha$ for every $0<\alpha<d$ [@hutchcroft-hierarchical-2021], and the volume exponent satisfies $\delta\geq rac{d+\alpha}{d-\alpha}$ above the triangle threshold, with equality conjectured. The classical long-range values are tabulated by Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972]; the rigorous versions in the mean-field region are due to Aizenman and Fernandez [@aizenman-fernandez-1988]. title: The Bleher–Sinai fixed point
subtitle: Above the threshold a non-Gaussian law is self-similar, and its multiplier is not one over alpha.
summary: For kernel exponent above half the dimension the critical orbit of the hierarchical recursion converges to a self-similar law that is not Gaussian: the fixed point of Bleher and Sinai and of Gawedzki and Kupiainen. Its linearisation has a simple leading eigenvalue, which gives a correlation-length exponent different from the classical one over alpha, and a spectrum whose next eigenvalue controls corrections to scaling, sometimes oscillating.
text:
For $\alpha$ above half the dimension the critical orbit of the hierarchical recursion does not settle at a Gaussian law. It converges instead to a self-similar law $
u^*$ which is symmetric, has exponential tails and finite variance, and is not Gaussian; the multiplier of the linearised map there is a number $\lambda_1>1$ other than $L^{\alpha}$, and the correlation-length exponent $
u=\log L/\log\lambda_1$ therefore differs from the classical value $1/\alpha$. The existence of such a law, the convergence of the orbit to it, and the reading of the indices from the linearisation are the results of Bleher and Sinai (1973, 1975) for Dyson's model [@bleher-sinai-1973] [@bleher-sinai-1975]; the local analysis of the map around the fixed point, including the $\varepsilon$-expansion and the normal form of the unstable manifold, is due to Gawedzki and Kupiainen [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. The threshold $\alpha=d/2$ is where the classical long-range exponents stop being the Ising ones. At $\alpha=d/2$ the classical values are $
u=2/d$, $\eta=2-d/2$, $\delta=3$ and $ eta_{\mathrm{o}}=	frac12$, which are the mean-field values with $
u$ adjusted by hyperscaling; below it the classical values hold, and above it the nontrivial fixed point takes over. In the language of the exponent dictionary the growth exponent is still $\kappa=\alpha$, because the autonomy of the recursion fixes it, and what changes is $
u$ alone. Two features make this the hard case and the reason the hierarchical model is worth studying. The fixed point is not explicit: it is the solution of a nonlinear integral equation, and its existence is proved by a combination of an invariant cone, a truncation and a contraction. And the map is not contracting everywhere: the leading eigenvalue exceeds one, so the interesting statement is about the unstable manifold of dimension two, which is what makes the critical exponents well defined at all. The rest of this article states the theorem, gives the mechanism of its proof, and describes the spectrum. The decimation operator $\mathcal T_b$ and its rescaled form $\mathcal R_{	heta,b}$ act on $\mathcal E$ when they are defined, and the model's orbit is $
u_n=\mathcal R_{	heta_0,b_1}^{\,n}
u_0$ with $	heta_0=	frac12(d+\alpha)$ and $b_1= eta J_1$ by the autonomous form . The critical coupling $b_c=b_c(m,\lambda)$ is the value of $b$ at which the orbit of the Ising initial law $
u_0=	frac12(\delta_{-1}+\delta_1)$ under $\mathcal R_{	heta_0,b}$ neither converges to the point mass at $0$ nor leaves every compact set of laws with bounded variance; it is the value $b_c= eta_cJ_1$ at which $ eta_c$ is the critical intensity of the model. The Gaussian laws form an invariant family, and the fixed points of the rescaled map inside that family are computed by one line of algebra. The computation is the reference point for everything else, so it is stated first. Let $b>0$ and $	heta=	frac12(d+\alpha)$. At $b=b_1^{(0)}=\dfrac{\lambda-m}{\lambda(m-1)}$ this fixed point is $N(0,1)$ and the multiplier of $\mathcal R_{	heta,b}$ in the variance direction is $\lambda/m=L^{\alpha}$. title: Hierarchical models with continuous symmetry
subtitle: With a vector spin the block direction does not settle at criticality, and the marginal exponent is decided by a slowly varying factor.
summary: For the r-component hierarchical model the decimation map acts on laws on R^r by the same tilt, and it commutes with rotations. Bleher and Major proved Dyson's conjecture for this model: at the marginal kernel exponent a transition exists exactly when the level couplings are not summable, the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes at the critical temperature, and the normalised average spin still converges to the uniform law on the sphere. The Gaussian fixed point is r-independent; the continuous symmetry enters through a marginal angular direction.
text:
The $r$-component hierarchical model is the model of the decimation article with a vector spin: $\sigma_x\in\mathbb R^r$ and energy $-\sum_{\{x,y\}}J(\lVert x-yVert)\langle\sigma_x,\sigma_yangle$, with $J(L^n)=l_nL^{-(d+\alpha)n}$. Rotation invariance replaces the spin-flip symmetry, the block spin becomes a vector, and the decimation identity survives with inner products in place of products; what does not survive is the scalar picture of criticality. At the critical temperature the direction of the block spin does not concentrate: Bleher and Major proved that the normalised average spin converges in law to the uniform distribution on the sphere, while the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes [@bleher-major-2021]. The same work settles Dyson's conjecture for this model at the marginal exponent. When $\alpha=d$ the interaction is summable or not according to the level sequence: $\sum_nJ_nL^{dn}=\sum_nl_n$. Bleher and Major prove that a phase transition exists exactly when $\sum_nl_n=\infty$, so the marginal case is decided by the slowly varying factor and not by any exponent, and they prove that the transition is continuous — there is no Thouless effect, in which the magnetisation would jump. What replaces the jump is the failure of concentration of the direction at criticality: the order parameter is zero, and yet the block spin is not small. Two structural facts organise the comparison with the scalar case. The decimation map commutes with rotations, so the state of the recursion is a rotation-covariant law on $\mathbb R^r$; and the Gaussian fixed point is $r$-independent, since the tilt couples the components separately and the variance recursion is the scalar one. The exponents $\kappa=\alpha$ and $\eta=2-\alpha$ are therefore unchanged by $r$, and the $r$-dependence enters through a marginal angular direction, the hierarchical counterpart of a Goldstone mode, which is what the nontrivial fixed point acquires when the symmetry is continuous. title: The phi-fourth hierarchical model and its truncations
subtitle: The recursion is an integral operator on potentials; the Gaussian truncation is exact and every other truncation leaks.
summary: Written on potentials rather than on laws, the decimation step is an explicit integral operator: the effective potential of a block is minus the logarithm of a constrained convolution of the child potential. Quadratic potentials are mapped to quadratic potentials and the flow on them is the fractional linear recursion for the variance; quartic and higher truncations are not invariant, because the constrained average of a quartic generates powers of every even order. The two rigorous treatments of the resulting infinite-dimensional flow are Koch and Wittwer's fixed point and, in the Euclidean setting, the trajectory of Abdesselam.
text: In the hierarchical model with a spin prior of the form $e^{-V(s)}ds$ the state of the recursion is a potential, not a number: after one decimation step the block spin has a density whose negative logarithm is the effective potential , computed from the child potential by a constrained convolution. The recursion is exact and it is an operation on an infinite-dimensional space; the question is which finite-dimensional families it leaves invariant, and the answer is that only the quadratic one does. Write $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2+\lambda s^4$; the Gaussian part flows by a fractional linear recursion solved in the Gaussian article , and the quartic part generates powers of every even order, so a two-coupling truncation is an approximation whose error is not controlled by the recursion itself [@bleher-sinai-1973]. The two rigorous treatments of the full flow are Koch and Wittwer's proof of a nontrivial fixed point for scalar hierarchical models [@koch-wittwer-1986], described in this wiki's article on it , and, in the Euclidean setting, Abdesselam's construction of a complete trajectory between the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points [@abdesselam-2007], described in the article on that . The hierarchical recursion is the one-dimensional iteration which Abdesselam's construction perturbs, so the potential formulation of this article is where the two meet. The quartic coupling is relevant exactly when the kernel exponent is above half the dimension, which is the hierarchical form of the upper critical dimension: for $\alpha<d/2$ the interaction is long enough that the Gaussian fixed point governs, and for $\alpha>d/2$ the nontrivial fixed point does. The values $\alpha=d/2$ and, for short-range models, $d=4$, are the same statement in the parametrisation of Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972]. Definitions and setting # Let $V$ be even, bounded below, with $\int e^{-V(s)}ds 0$. The hierarchical model with prior $e^{-V(s)}ds$ has the decimation recursion of the decimation article , and its block-spin law has a density because the tilt and the convolution of a density are densities. For $b\geq0$ the effective potential $\mathcal V_bV$ is defined by $$e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)(s)}=\frac{1}{Z_b(V)}\int_{\mathbb R^{m-1}}\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}\Bigr)\prod_{a=1}^{m-1}e^{-V(s_a)}\,ds_1\cdots ds_{m-1},$$ with $s_m=s-\sum_{a<m}s_a$, and the scaled potential at exponent $\theta$ is $(\mathcal R_\theta V)(s)=(\mathcal V_bV)(L^{\theta}s)$ up to an additive constant. The potential formulation and the law formulation of the map article carry the same information: $e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)}$ is the density of $\mathcal T_b(e^{-V}ds)$. The constant in front is fixed by normalisation and plays no role in the flow of the shape of the potential; additive constants are the free energy increments of the free energy recursion and are dropped from the potential from here on. The Gaussian truncation # The one family the recursion preserves is the quadratic one, and on it the recursion is explicit. Let $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2$ with $\mu>0$ and $b<1/(v(m-1))$, where $v=1/\mu$. Then $\mathcal V_bV$ is quadratic, with curvature $\mu'$ given by $$\frac{1}{\mu'}=\frac{m}{\mu-b(m-1)},$$ that is $\mu'=(\mu-b(m-1))/m$: the curvature flows affinely, and the variance recursion $v'=mv/(1-bv(m-1))$ is the same statement for $v=1/\mu$. A quartic potential is not mapped to a quartic potential: at $\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2+\lambda s^4$ with $\lambda\neq0$ the first and second orders in $\lambda$ are again quartics in $s$, but the third order is not, and a sixth power appears with a coefficient proportional to $\lambda^3$. title: Koch and Wittwer's non-Gaussian fixed point
subtitle: Convergent expansions for a fixed point with unbounded spins, large fields included.
summary: Koch and Wittwer proved the existence of a non-Gaussian fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map, in the hierarchical approximation of the three-dimensional phi-fourth fixed point, by a method that treats the large-field region: Borel summation brings the region where the perturbative expansion fails back into it, so that the theory is described by convergent expansions. The companion papers study the transformation itself, with its beta function and the relation between Dyson's and Gallavotti's hierarchies, and treat the Dyson-Baker hierarchy.
text: A fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map that is not quadratic is the critical theory of the scalar model above the marginal exponent, and the two general routes to it leave a gap. The theorem of Bleher and Sinai proves existence in a class of measures, but its statement is qualitative and its hypotheses are those of a parameter range; the epsilon expansion of Gawedzki and Kupiainen describes a neighbourhood of the marginal exponent. Koch and Wittwer closed the gap for the hierarchical model with unbounded spins by proving that the non-Gaussian fixed point governing the infrared behaviour of the three-dimensional critical theory exists, and that the theory around it is described by convergent expansions [@koch-wittwer-1986]. The obstacle they had to remove is the large-field problem . With a phi-fourth single-spin distribution the spins are unbounded, and the region in which the field is large carries most of the measure while lying outside the reach of the perturbative expansion; a renormalisation-group argument that controls the small-field region alone does not define the map. Their method handles that region by Borel summation, which resums the perturbation series so that the large-field region is incorporated into the perturbative one, and improves on the analyticity techniques of Gawedzki and Kupiainen's hierarchy-model papers [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1982] [@gawedzki-kupiainen-tirozzi-1984]. The result is a fixed point with a convergent expansion around it, at a specific parameter value and without a small parameter. The two companion papers complete the picture. The paper of 1991 studies the renormalisation transformation for scalar hierarchical models as an object in its own right: the beta function written for the transformation, its asymptotic behaviour, and the connection between the hierarchical models of Dyson and of Gallavotti [@koch-wittwer-1991]. The paper of 1994 proves a nontrivial fixed point for the Dyson-Baker hierarchical model, the variant whose blocks come from an expanding map of the interval [@koch-wittwer-1994]. Definitions and setting # The object is the effective-potential map of the truncations article : for a potential $V$ and a coupling $b\geq0$, $$e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)(s)}=\int_{\mathbb R^{m-1}}\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}\Bigr)\prod_{a=1}^{m}e^{-V(s_a)}\,ds_1\cdots ds_{m-1},\qquad s_m=s-\sum_{a<m}s_a,$$ with the normalising constant dropped. The model is the hierarchical approximation of a three-dimensional lattice field theory with a phi-fourth interaction: the block sums of the hierarchy play the role of the block averages of the lattice, and the fixed point of the map is the critical theory of the approximation. A fixed point is a potential $V^*$ with $\mathcal V_bV^*=V^*$ up to an additive constant, and the problem is to find one that is not quadratic. The quadratic fixed point exists for exactly one curvature at each coupling, is computed in the Gaussian article , and is the fixed point that loses stability at the marginal exponent; the non-quadratic fixed point is the one that takes over. Because the single-spin distribution has unbounded support, the domain of the map is not a space of bounded functions: the tilt and the constraint allow configurations in which one child carries an arbitrarily large spin, and the integral defining $\mathcal V_bV$ is finite only because the prior decays. The large-field region is the part of the domain of integration in which some $\lvert s_a\rvert$ exceeds a scale at which the perturbative expansion is valid, and controlling it is a precondition for the map to be defined at all as an operation on a space of potentials. title: Abdesselam's trajectory between two fixed points
subtitle: A whole orbit of the renormalisation group, from the Gaussian fixed point to the nontrivial one.
summary: A fixed point describes one scale-invariant theory; a trajectory between two fixed points describes the whole crossover from the ultraviolet to the infrared. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for a three-dimensional phi-fourth model with modified propagator, joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, by a fixed point argument in a Banach space of sequences which perturbs a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration.
text: The renormalisation group of a lattice field theory is a map on a space of interactions, one step per scale, and most rigorous results about it are local: a fixed point, its stable and unstable manifolds, and the behaviour of orbits near it. A complete trajectory is a global object instead, an orbit defined at every scale and asymptotic at one end to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point and at the other to the nontrivial infrared one. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for the three-dimensional $\varphi^4$ model with a modified free propagator [@abdesselam-2007], joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point of the kind constructed by Brydges, Mitter and Scoppola [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003]. Two features of the construction matter for this wiki. It does not use the hierarchical approximation — the map is the Euclidean one — and yet the unperturbed problem it perturbs is a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration of exactly the kind the hierarchical model provides, with the perturbation supplied by the modified propagator [@abdesselam-2009]. The hierarchical recursion is therefore not an analogy for the Euclidean renormalisation group in this work but its first approximation, and the trajectory is recovered from the one-dimensional flow by a fixed-point argument in a space of sequences of effective potentials. The modification of the propagator is what makes the argument close: it suppresses the fluctuations at each scale by a fixed amount, so that the Euclidean step is a bounded perturbation of the hierarchical one. Whether the trajectory can be transported to the unmodified propagator is a separate question, and the construction is a statement about the modified model. Definitions and setting # The renormalisation group is the following operation, in the form used in the renormalisation-group treatment of lattice fields [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. One fixes a fluctuation covariance $C$, a positive definite kernel on the lattice, and a decomposition of it into pieces $C=\sum_jC_j$ indexed by scale. Given an effective potential $V_j$ at scale $j$, one defines $$e^{-V_{j+1}(\varphi)}=\int e^{-V_j(\varphi+\zeta)}\,\mu_{C_j}(d\zeta),$$ the convolution of the Boltzmann weight with the Gaussian measure of covariance $C_j$, followed by the rescalings of field and position that put the result in a fixed normal form. The map $V_j\mapsto V_{j+1}$ is the renormalisation step, and a fixed point of the step is a scale-invariant theory. A trajectory between two fixed points is a sequence $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ of effective potentials, each in the domain of the map, such that $V_{j+1}$ is the image of $V_j$ for every $j$, and such that $V_j$ converges to the Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The first limit is the ultraviolet, the second the infrared; the intermediate potentials describe the crossover, which is the region in which neither fixed point's linearisation controls the flow. For the hierarchical model the corresponding object is a sequence of laws $\nu_j=\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}^{\,j}\nu_0$ under the single map of the autonomous form , and a trajectory between fixed points is an orbit whose two ends are the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points of that map. In that case the trajectory is a property of a one-dimensional iteration and can be analysed by the methods of the fixed-point article . Statement # Let the field be three-dimensional with a modified free propagator, and let the interaction be a $\varphi^4$ perturbation with a small coupling. Then there is a sequence of effective potentials $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ satisfying the renormalisation recursion exactly, asymptotic to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial infrared fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. title: Renormalisation for hierarchical percolation
subtitle: Cluster amplification is the relevant direction, and the triangle threshold is three alpha against d.
summary: For long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice the renormalisation group acts on clusters rather than on a one-variable law, and its relevant direction is the amplification of large clusters across a block. The critical two-point function decays like the distance to the power minus d minus alpha for every exponent in the long-range range, and the triangle diagram converges exactly when three alpha is below d, which is where the model stops being mean-field.
text: Long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice has bond intensities $J\lVert x-y\rVert^{-d-\alpha}$, so the intensity of the edge between two vertices depends only on their level, and the model inherits the child decomposition of the lattice. Its renormalisation group does not act on the law of one number: the state of a block is the partition of its vertices into clusters, and the operation of decimation is the passage from the cluster partition of the children to that of the block. What survives from the spin case is the amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined with probability comparable to $\beta J_n$ times their product of sizes, so a block whose clusters are atypically large produces a parent whose clusters are larger still. That mechanism gives the exact exponents. At criticality the expected size of the restricted cluster of the origin in $\Lambda_n$ grows like $L^{\alpha n}$ — the growth exponent $\kappa=\alpha$ of the exponent dictionary — and the critical connection probability between vertices at distance $L^n$ is of order $L^{-(d-\alpha)n}$, so $\eta=2-\alpha$ for every $0<\alpha<d$. This is unambiguous in the mean-field region, where the second moment of the cluster size diverges, and it holds beyond it as well; the theorem is Hutchcroft's, and it is the only case in which the two-point exponent is known across the whole long-range range [@hutchcroft-hierarchical-2021]. The phase transition itself is classical: $\beta_c$ is finite exactly when $\alpha<d$, and there is no infinite cluster at $\beta_c$ [@koval-meester-trapman-2012]. The renormalisation group enters at the level of exponents, and the question it answers is why the model is mean-field below $\alpha=d/3$ and not above: the triangle diagram is a convergent sum below that value and a divergent one above it, and the diagram is computable here because the lattice is ultrametric. Definitions and setting # Let $0<\alpha<d$, $\beta\geq0$, and for distinct $x,y\in\mathbb H^d_L$ declare the pair an open edge independently with probability $p_\beta(x,y)=1-e^{-\beta J\lVert x-y\rVert^{-d-\alpha}}$. The cluster $K_x$ is the set of vertices joined to $x$ by open paths, $K^{\Lambda_n}_x$ is the same object computed with edges inside $\Lambda_n$, and $$\tau_\beta(x,y)=\mathbb P_\beta(x\leftrightarrow y),\qquad \tau^{\Lambda_n}_\beta(x,y)=\mathbb P_\beta\bigl(x\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda_n}y\bigr),\qquad \chi_n(\beta)=\mathbb E_\beta\lvert K^{\Lambda_n}_0\rvert .$$ The critical intensity is $\beta_c=\inf\{\beta:\mathbb P_\beta(\lvert K_0\rvert=\infty)>0\}$, and $\chi_n$ is the block susceptibility of the exponent article . Two auxiliary quantities are used below: the level-$n$ quantile $$R_n(\beta)=\min\bigl\{r\geq1:\mathbb P_\beta\bigl(\max_{x\in\Lambda_n}\lvert K^{\Lambda_n}_x\rvert\geq r\bigr)\leq e^{-1}\bigr\},$$ the typical size of the largest cluster of a block, and the amplification factor $\beta J_n=\beta JL^{-(d+\alpha)n}$, which is the intensity of every edge joining two distinct children of $\Lambda_n$. Two exact recursion inequalities # The percolation analogue of the decimation identity is a pair of inequalities, both exact consequences of the child decomposition and the independence of the bonds between children. Let $n\geq0$, let $B,B'$ be distinct children of $\Lambda_{n+1}$, let $x\in B$ and $y\in B'$, and let $I=\lvert K^{B}_x\rvert$ and $I'=\lvert K^{B'}_y\rvert$ computed with the bonds inside $B$ and $B'$ respectively. Then the pair $(I,I')$ is independent and $$\tau^{\Lambda_{n+1}}_\beta(x,y)\ \geq\ \mathbb E_\beta\bigl[1-e^{-\beta J_{n+1}II'}\bigr].$$ Proof of the one-edge bound Children are disjoint and every edge joining them is at level $n+1$, so the bonds of $B$ and of $B'$ are disjoint sets and $(I,I')$ is a pair of independent random variables, each with the law of the restricted cluster size in the model on $\Lambda_n$ with free boundary. title: Hierarchical and Euclidean renormalisation
subtitle: Why the recursion closes here, what fails on the lattice, and how the model is used anyway.
summary: The hierarchical recursion is exact because a block has no boundary: all pairs between two children carry one coupling, so the decimated state is a function of the child states alone. On the Euclidean lattice a block has a boundary of codimension one, the effective interaction after decimation depends on the geometry of the boundary and not on block sums, and the decimated measure need not be Gibbsian. The hierarchical model is nevertheless the reference for power counting, for the epsilon expansion and for the local analysis of the renormalisation map.
text: The decimation identity is an identity, and not an approximation, because of one geometric fact: any two vertices in different children of a hierarchical block are at the same distance, so every pair joining two children carries the same coupling and the interaction between them is a function of the two block sums. A block has no boundary in the sense that no pair of its vertices is closer to the outside than another, and its children are congruent copies of itself. The recursion therefore closes on the law of one number. On $\mathbb Z^d$ none of this holds. A cube of side $L^n$ has a boundary of codimension one: the fraction of pairs at distance of order $L^n$ that join two neighbouring blocks is small, the number of nearest-neighbour edges crossing the boundary is of order $L^{(d-1)n}$ rather than $L^{dn}$, and the interaction between two blocks depends on whether they share a face, an edge or a corner. After one decimation step the effective interaction between two block magnetisations is a sum over a boundary whose size depends on the pair, and after two steps the interaction acquires a dependence on the shape of the interface. There is no finite-dimensional family of interactions closed under the operation, and there is a stronger obstruction: the decimated measure of a Gibbs measure need not be Gibbsian at all [@van-enter-fernandez-sokal-1993]. What the hierarchical model supplies in spite of this is the local structure of the renormalisation map itself: its fixed points, the dimension of the unstable manifold, the eigenvalue problem, the $\varepsilon$-expansion about the upper critical exponent, and the mechanism by which the nonlinearity is irrelevant [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. Those are the inputs of the Euclidean renormalisation group, and the hierarchical model is the setting in which they can be established; the transfer is the programme of Gawedzki and Kupiainen for lattice field theory [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1980], and of the renormalisation-group analysis of critical $(\Phi^4)_3$ and related models [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003] [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. Definitions and setting # Let $L\geq2$. On the hierarchical lattice the level-$n$ block is the subgroup $\Lambda_n$ of the lattice article , its children are the cosets of $\Lambda_{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the law of the block spin $S_{\Lambda_n}$. On $\mathbb Z^d$ the level-$n$ block at $x$ is the cube $x+[0,L^n)^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, its children are the $L^d$ subcubes of side $L^{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the joint law of the $L^d$ block magnetisations of the children together with the fine configuration inside them. An interaction is a function $\Phi$ on configurations; a decimation step maps the Gibbs measure with interaction $\Phi$ on the fine lattice to the law of the coarse variables. A family of interactions is closed if the decimated measure is again a Gibbs measure with an interaction in the family, for every member of the family and every choice of the coarse-graining scale. What closes the recursion # Suppose that a block $B$ is the disjoint union of $m$ children $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ and that the interaction is a sum over unordered pairs of a coupling that is constant on the set of pairs joining two given children. Then the energy of a configuration on $B$ is a function of the child configurations through the $m$ block sums alone, and the law of the $m$-tuple of block sums under the Gibbs measure of $B$ is determined by the interaction inside a child and by the $m(m-1)/2$ couplings between children. If in addition every child is isomorphic to $B$ with the same internal interaction, one decimation step is the map $\mathcal T_b$ of the map article , and the family of interactions on the scale of a block is closed. title: Abdesselam: from one fixed point to another
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for Abdesselam's work on trajectories of the renormalisation group. The group is small and its object is unusual: not a fixed point and not a local analysis around one, but a whole orbit of the exact renormalisation group, defined at every scale, joining the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point to a nontrivial infrared one. The construction is nonperturbative, it does not use the hierarchical approximation, and its unperturbed problem is nevertheless a one-dimensional iteration of the kind the hierarchical model supplies - which is why it belongs in this wiki. The wiki states this as the theorem of the trajectory article, with the two endpoints and the exactness of the recursion as its content, and with the modified propagator recorded as a hypothesis rather than suppressed: the trajectory is a statement about the modified model. What the wiki does not do is reproduce the estimates. The mechanism is described in the terms the account of the construction uses - a one-dimensional unperturbed problem, a small perturbation supplied by the propagator, and a weighted space of sequences in which the recursion is a contraction - and the norms themselves are left to the paper. The 2009 account: the method This is where the relation to the hierarchical model is stated in the form the wiki uses: the renormalisation group map is defined rigorously and nonperturbatively without the hierarchical approximation, and the trajectories are constructed by perturbing a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration. That sentence is the quantitative version of the comparison drawn in the article on hierarchical and Euclidean renormalisation, and the wiki cites this account for it. The 2018 programme: why the ultrametric case matters If a three-dimensional conformal field theory is to be constructed by renormalisation-group methods, the setting in which the block structure is exact is the natural testing ground. The paper develops the ultrametric and p-adic versions of the model with that end in view. The wiki uses it only for the variants: the p-adic and ultrametric models as members of the same class, and the reason the class is worth having. title: Bleher, Major and Sinai: the hierarchical model and its exponents
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for the group of works that made Dyson's hierarchical model the standard laboratory of the renormalisation group. The division of labour is clear enough to state in one paragraph. Bleher and Sinai turned the block-spin recursion into a nonlinear transformation of probability measures and computed the critical indices from its linearisation; Bleher then constructed self-similar fields with hierarchical structure, which are the fixed points of the transformation in the language of random fields; Bleher and Major extended the analysis to vector spins, to the ordered phase with its limit theorems, and to the marginal exponent at which the criterion for a transition becomes a condition on the level sequence; and Sinai's monograph is the systematic account of the framework of limit Gibbs distributions in which the model sits. The wiki uses the group in three ways: as the source of the recursion and of the fixed-point theorem, as the source of the exponent values and their status, and as the source of the phenomena that distinguish the vector from the scalar case. No technical estimate of these papers is reconstructed here; statements are attributed to the works that establish them. title: Koch and Wittwer: the large-field problem
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for the three papers in which Hans Koch and Peter Wittwer proved that the hierarchical renormalisation map has a nontrivial fixed point with unbounded spins. The group is small and unusually homogeneous: the same two authors, one object, four papers, and a method that is the reason the papers are cited. The method is not a numerical certification. It is an analytic treatment of the large-field region , the part of the integral defining the effective potential in which the spin is too large for the perturbative expansion to converge and which, for an unbounded single-spin distribution, carries a non-negligible part of the measure. Borel summation resums the series there and brings the region back inside a convergent expansion. The point of the group, for this wiki, is that it closes the gap between the two other general treatments: the theorem of Bleher and Sinai gives existence in a class of measures with a qualitative statement and a parameter range, and the epsilon expansion of Gawedzki and Kupiainen describes a neighbourhood of the marginal exponent. Koch and Wittwer prove the fixed point of the hierarchical approximation of the three-dimensional theory, with convergent expansions around it, without a small parameter. The mechanism the wiki describes is the one the paper's own summary gives: the large-field region is the obstacle, Borel summation is what removes it, and the technique is an improvement of the analyticity methods of Gawedzki and Kupiainen's hierarchy-model papers. The wiki does not attempt to reproduce the estimates, and it separates two claims that the literature sometimes runs together: the existence of the fixed point, which is this paper, and the one-dimensional instability that makes it critical, which is the general theory and the companion paper.
